title: Why America Can’t Strangle Iran
gist: Iran's economy is in severe financial distress — a projected 5.4 percent GDP contraction, 88.6 percent inflation, a rial past two million to the dollar — but the author argues U.S. policymakers misread these headline numbers: Tehran deliberately chose austerity and inflation to push the cost of sanctions and war onto households and firms, and deep corporate inventories plus repressive capacity mean the state can absorb the pain for years without capitulating.

insights.claim: The IMF estimated in July that Iran's GDP will contract 5.4 percent this year, after shrinking by less than half that over the previous 12 months.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Sets the base rate for how much contraction the Islamic Republic has already proven it can absorb without policy change.
insights.locator: According to a July estimate by the International Monetary Fund

insights.claim: Iranian year-on-year inflation climbed from 52.6 percent in December 2025 to 88.6 percent by the start of summer 2026, and the rial hit a record low of over two million to the dollar.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: The relevant threshold is not these levels but monthly inflation above 50 percent; until then the strategy holds.
insights.locator: Year-on-year inflation climbed from 52.6 percent

insights.claim: U.S. and Israeli airstrikes have hit critical Iranian industrial facilities including major steel and petrochemical plants, causing production outages for key industrial goods, while the naval blockade and falling Hormuz traffic have throttled imports of capital and consumer goods as well as exports.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: War is doing what a decade of sanctions could not — destroying physical capacity — which matters more for Iranian output than financial measures do.
insights.locator: Today, war is testing the resilience of the Iranian economy

insights.claim: Iranian imports totaled $17 billion in the first five months of the Iranian calendar year beginning in March, implying roughly $40 billion for the year versus $58 billion the previous year and $72 billion the year before that.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: A 45 percent import collapse in two years is the clearest read on Iranian demand destruction — and a direct hit to Gulf and Turkish re-export trade.
insights.locator: Iran’s foremost vulnerability to sanctions and the blockade

themes.theme: Why pressure fails: the pain is transferred, not absorbed

insights.claim: Trump's economic campaign can immiserate most of Iran's people but cannot strangle the Islamic Republic itself, because the state has figured out how to offload economic pain onto ordinary Iranians while meeting its own needs.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: The core trade implication: do not price Iranian regime capitulation or a sanctions-driven settlement off macro deterioration alone.
insights.quote: Trump’s approach, in other words, can certainly immiserate most of the country’s people. But it cannot successfully strangle the Islamic Republic itself.
insights.locator: But even as the country’s economic situation is getting worse

insights.claim: Iranian leaders publicly lamenting popular suffering are not signaling imminent collapse; they are dissenting from a long-standing elite consensus that deliberately pushes sanctions pressure onto ordinary people, so U.S. officials citing those statements as evidence of success are overinterpreting them.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: A direct warning that Washington's success metrics are reading elite rhetoric backwards — expect policy surprise when pressure does not produce capitulation.
insights.quote: Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian are complaining about the social costs of a policy response that has worked largely as intended.
insights.locator: The statements from Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian

insights.claim: Macroeconomic indicators such as growth, inflation and currency depreciation give only a financial view of a sanctioned economy; a functional view requires firm- and household-level data, which is why deteriorating headline figures have not produced Iranian capitulation.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: A reusable model for assessing any sanctioned economy — Russia, Venezuela, Syria — that separates price-level distress from functional capacity.
insights.quote: They provide, in other words, a financial—not a functional—view of the economy.
insights.locator: Perhaps more important, U.S. assessments

insights.claim: A comprehensively sanctioned country facing balance-of-payments stress has two options: expansionary policy to rebuild the trade surplus through higher output, or monetary tightening and austerity to suppress import demand — Russia chose the first and Iran chose the second.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Explains why Russian and Iranian economies behave so differently under sanctions and predicts where each breaks first.
insights.locator: The fundamental dilemma for policymakers

insights.claim: Russia's fiscal stimulus after invading Ukraine built a war economy that tightened the labor market and raised real wages, blunting sanctions-related inflation and allowing Russia to persist in its war aims — though that approach has now reached its limits and inflation is starting to bite.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Flags Russian inflation as the live constraint on Moscow's war economy, in contrast to Iran where inflation is the chosen tool.
insights.locator: When faced with major sanctions after invading Ukraine

insights.claim: Iran's 'resistance economy' was never implemented as industrial policy or a welfare system; officials instead tolerated inflation, ran austerity budgets and refused quotas or price controls, which pushed the cost of sanctions from the government onto households and firms and enabled employer wage repression.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Identifies Iranian household consumption, not state finances, as the shock absorber — so consumer-facing sectors deteriorate long before the state does.
insights.locator: Iranian officials, by contrast, chose the second course

insights.claim: Iranian authorities are content to see economic activity slow because they believe contraction gives them staying power in the confrontation with the United States.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Reframes weak Iranian data as an intended outcome rather than a pressure point, removing the main assumed channel of U.S. leverage.
insights.locator: At first, this may seem like a policy failure

insights.claim: Iranian listed companies hold average days-inventory-outstanding of around three months, and in heavily restricted sectors such as electrical machinery inventories run as high as 200 days.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: A quantified estimate of how long Iranian industry can operate through a blockade — the single most useful number for timing supply-side stress.
insights.quote: In sensitive sectors such as electrical machinery, which has been heavily targeted by U.S. restrictions, firms maintain inventories as high as 200 days.
insights.locator: According to filings made by companies listed

insights.claim: Iranian firms built the habit of large inventories over two decades because stockpiles both mitigate sanctions-driven supply chain shocks and protect balance sheets in a high-inflation environment where cash loses value but goods do not.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: A generalizable behavior: inflationary, sanctioned economies convert working capital into goods, which makes reported inventory levels a solvency indicator rather than a warning sign.
insights.locator: But that does not mean these firms are insolvent

insights.claim: In functional terms Iranian inventory levels are unchanged from December 2025 even though the economy is financially worse off, suggesting supply and demand may simply settle at a lower level of overall activity.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: The economy is finding a lower equilibrium rather than approaching a cliff — argues against pricing a near-term Iranian breakdown.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, reduced economic activity has provided buffers

insights.claim: Iran's Chamber of Commerce PMI data show the overall economy in contraction for two-thirds of the 2019-2023 period, yet non-oil industries grew modestly throughout, and by March 2024 living standards were rising again on a roughly 15 percent increase in real incomes.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Evidence that sanctions alone were losing effectiveness before the war — pressure only bit once military strikes began.
insights.locator: GOOD TIMES, BAD TIMES

insights.claim: The April 2024 Israeli airstrikes, not sanctions, derailed Iran's recovery, and recurring military conflict has since produced eight consecutive months of deteriorating industrial conditions.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Attributes the inflection to kinetic risk, meaning any de-escalation — not sanctions relief — is what would restart Iranian industrial activity.
insights.locator: This recovery was derailed by the April 2024 Israeli airstrikes

insights.claim: Iranian firms passed higher input costs into prices to protect margins, causing demand destruction that has forced households into consumer credit including buy-now-pay-later schemes and informal loans, with retailers reporting falling volumes even in food.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Household credit growth in a hyperinflating economy is a forward indicator of social stress — the metric to watch for protest risk.
insights.locator: Firms kept raising prices to protect their margins

insights.claim: Unlike during the Iran-Iraq War, when price controls successfully blunted economic pain, the government has refused price controls and has discussed eliminating cash transfers and energy subsidies for large parts of the population, using demand destruction as a de facto rationing mechanism.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Subsidy removal in an 88 percent inflation environment is the most plausible trigger for renewed mass protest — a discrete event risk with a policy tell.
insights.locator: The sharp drop in household consumption

insights.claim: With monthly inflation under ten percent, Iran remains far from the hyperinflation threshold of over 50 percent monthly that would make the government's strategy untenable.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit, monitorable trigger level for when the Iranian strategy breaks — monthly, not annual, inflation.
insights.locator: With a monthly inflation rate of under ten percent

themes.theme: What Washington is actually up against

insights.claim: Iran avoided the runaway collapse seen in Syria and Venezuela partly because currency devaluation reduced import competition and made Iranian products more competitive in regional markets, boosting non-oil exports.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Devaluation acts as an automatic stabilizer for sanctioned industrial economies — a reason sanctions-driven currency collapse is self-limiting.
insights.locator: Its non-oil industries also adapted to the sanctions

insights.claim: Successfully strangling Iran would require asphyxiating 25 million households and more than one million firms, and even then ample oxygen would remain for the country's elite.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Frames maximum pressure as structurally incapable of achieving its stated objective — argue for a long Iran stalemate rather than a resolution.
insights.quote: To prevail in its economic war, the Trump administration will thus need to asphyxiate 25 million households and more than one million firms.
insights.locator: LOW POWER MODE

insights.claim: The transfer of sanctions and war costs onto ordinary Iranians is itself a form of wartime mobilization, and the repressive tools available to the state mean protest would again be met with violence rather than producing political change.
insights.speaker: Esfandyar Batmanghelidj
insights.so_what: Discounts the 'the people will rise up' scenario that underpins U.S. regime-change assumptions, and therefore the probability of a quick Iran risk-premium unwind.
